item.title: Deterministic and stochastic optimization for solving large size inverse problems in image processing
item.description: Dans cette thèse on s’intéresse au problème des décompositions canoniques polyadiques de tenseurs d’ordre N potentiellement grands et sous différentes contraintes (non-négativité, aspect creux lié à une possible surestimation du rang du tenseur). Pour traiter ce problème, nous proposons trois nouvelles approches itératives différentes: deux approches déterministes dont une approche proximale, et une approche stochastique. La première approche étend les travaux de thèse de J-P. Royer au cas de tenseurs de dimension N. Dans l’approche stochastique, nous considérons pour la première fois dans le domaine des décompositions tensorielles, des algorithmes génétiques (mimétiques) dont principe général repose sur l’évolution d’une population de candidats. Dans le dernier type d’approche, nous avons considéré un algorithme proximal pré-conditionné (le Block-Coordinate Variable Metric Forward-Backward), algorithme fonctionnant par blocs de données avec une matrice de pré-conditionnement liée à chaque bloc et fondé sur deux étapes successives principales : une étape de gradient et une étape proximale. Finalement, les différentes méthodes suggérées sont comparées entre elles et avec d’autres algorithmes classiques de la littérature sur des données synthétiques (à la fois aléatoires ou proches des données observées en spectroscopie de fluorescence) et sur des données expérimentales réelles correspondant à une campagne de surveillance des eaux d’une rivière et visant à la détection d’apparition de polluants.

item.title: Novel computational workflow for selecting virtual patient cohorts for in silico clinical trials
item.description: Objectives: In silico clinical trials are a well-accepted model-informed drug development (MIDD) tool to understand, optimize and predict the effect of drugs across diverse populations [1,2]. Generation and selection of virtual patients for simulating in silico trials remains an open area of research not least due to challenges of selecting virtual patients that are representative of the underlying physiological and clinical characteristics of individual subjects enrolled into clinical trials [3]. While virtual patients can be obtained by sampling sets of parameters from a calibrated non-linear mixed effects model, these may however generate biomarkers outside the expected range of observations, thus impacting the accuracy of in silico clinical trials predictions. To obtain a more representative virtual population, different algorithms can be applied to tailor plausible patient cohorts and yield calibrated virtual patients. In this work, we present a new virtual patient selection workflow using a minimal quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Methods: A QSP model of HBV disease progression incorporating the effect of standard-of-care therapies (peg-interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues) was used to generate plausible patient cohorts corresponding to the Everest trial [4] (a real-world clinical study exploring how interferon therapy can achieve functional cure in chronically infected patients). To tailor plausible patients to a virtual cohort mimicking baseline characteristics of patients enrolled into the Everest project, we developed a computational algorithm based on a mixed-integer linear programming framework coupled to a multi-objective optimization genetic algorithm. Subsequently, the virtual patient cohort obtained with this algorithm was used to perform in silico clinical trials mirroring the Everest protocol to validate the workflow. Non-linear relationships between baseline characteristics, prognostic biomarkers, and dosing parameters with clinical endpoints were explored using in silico trials. Results: We show that: (1) the HBV QSP model captures longitudinal biomarker data from untreated patients as well as chronically infected subjects receiving standard-of-care therapies, (2) Plausible patients generated with the model capture HBV disease progression, (3) The novel computational workflow efficiently selects virtual patients matching HBsAg and viral load baseline Everest data distributions, (4) In silico trials that mirrored the Everest trial showed quantitative agreement with clinical end-points thus validating the workflow, (5) In silico trials were leveraged to identify and compare optimal dosing regimens and explore mechanistic pathways in responders and non-responders to interferon. Conclusions: This work proposes and validates a novel QSP-based computational workflow for performing in silico trials, generating mechanistic hypotheses, and identifying optimal dosing regimens.Citations: COI: DW, AN, AS, RD are employees of and hold shares in GSK. item.title: G lobal
item.description: For modeling imprecise and indeterminate data for multi-objective decision making, two different methods: neutrosophic multi-objective linear/non-linear programming neutrosophic goal programming, which have been very recently proposed in the literatuire. In many economic problems, the well-known probabilities or fuzzy solutions procedures are not suitable because they cannot deal the situation when indeterminacy inherently involves in the problem. In this case we propose a new concept in optimization problem under uncertainty and indeterminacy. It is an extension of fuzzy and intuitionistic fuzzy optimization in which the degrees of indeterminacy and falsity (rejection) of objectives and constraints are simultaneously considered together with the degrees of truth membership (satisfaction/acceptance). The drawbacks of the existing neutrosophic optimization models have been presented and new framework of multi-objective optimization in neutrosophic environment has been proposed. The essence of the proposed approach is that it is capable of dealing with indeterminacy and falsity simultaneously.

item.title: Pediatric Tender Scheduling under uncertainty: A stochastic optimization approach
item.description: Pediatric vaccine tender scheduling is critical for ensuring long-term stability and equitable coverage in low- and lower-middle-income markets. Effective scheduling not only facilitates equitable vaccine procurement but also helps prevent the spread of vaccine-preventable diseases. However, the stochastic nature of demand and year-to-year supply fluctuations presents significant challenges to tender planning. This study aims to address three key questions: (1) What is the optimal sequencing and scheduling of vaccine tenders to enhance affordability and profitability over extended planning horizons? (2) How do ongoing tenders influence long-term scheduling strategies? (3) How does an optimized tender scheduling approach compare to current year-to-year decision-making practices? To answer these questions, we propose a stochastic optimization model that accounts for demand uncertainty and supply variability. Additionally, we develop a current-practice approximation model for benchmarking purposes. The study explores multiple optimization objectives, examining how different priorities impact tender length, duration, and scheduling. We also analyze the role of quantity discount pricing and its influence on tendering decisions. Through this analysis, we aim to provide actionable insights into tender scheduling and procurement strategies, offering practical guidelines for maximizing affordability and profitability. Our findings highlight the importance of incorporating existing tender commitments into long-term planning and provide evidence-based recommendations on scheduling and procurement policies. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a long-term planning horizon fosters sustainable vaccine coverage, enhancing both market stability and public health outcomes.

item.title: A Hybrid Last-Mile Delivery System Using a Truck and Diverse Robotic Fleet
item.description: The integration of autonomous robots into last-mile delivery systems offers a promising solution to the limitations of conventional truck-based logistics. This study investigates a hybrid last-mile delivery system utilizing both homogeneous and heterogeneous robots, addressing scenarios in urban areas. To manage battery constraints for robots returning after rendezvousing with a truck, we propose mixed-integer linear programming models that incorporate battery recharging and swapping strategies. Our work explores optimal solutions for truck and robot routes and evaluates different robot combinations to minimize total delivery time. We also develop a three-phased heuristic algorithm to efficiently solve large-scale problems. The models are validated using case studies in Ulsan Metropolitan City, South Korea. It demonstrates that the battery-swapping strategy can reduce total delivery time by up to 50% compared to truck-only systems. The findings highlight the significance of extended robot driving ranges in urban areas to enhance delivery performance. A sensitivity analysis further examines the effects of factors such as customer node size, robot speed, number of robots, and robot ratios. This study addresses key gaps in the literature on hybrid truck-robot delivery systems and provides practical insights to enhance efficiency and reduce delivery times in urban areas.

item.title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
item.description: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

item.title: manylp: reproducible, exact, and batched linear programming for genome-scale dynamic flux balance analysis
item.description: Dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) and its community, spatial and ensemble variants predict microbial metabolism by solving one linear program (LP) per species and time step, often 10^6 to 10^8 LPs per study. These LPs share their constraint matrix and objective and differ only in their bounds, yet general-purpose solvers treat each one independently, and GPU first-order solvers struggle with the degenerate, badly scaled matrices of genome-scale models. Moreover, metabolic optima are usually faces rather than vertices, so solvers return arbitrary flux vectors and dFBA predictions depend on the solver used. We present manylp, a batched solver for such bounds-parametric LP families that returns certified vertex solutions. Building on the bunching technique of stochastic programming, manylp caches optimal bases and certifies whole batches with one dense matrix product per basis on CPUs or GPUs; LPs outside the cached critical regions are re-solved by a warm-started lexicographic dual simplex, and new bases are propagated across the batch. Each LP is certified optimal and unique under a lexicographic flux rule, or infeasible, in independent double-precision arithmetic. On a genome-scale dFBA workload, manylp certified 47,889 LPs per second on a CPU, 12 to 33 times faster than HiGHS, Gurobi, FICO Xpress, GLPK and OR-Tools (32 processes), and reached 682,000 LPs per second on one GPU for community ensembles, needing 76 simplex solves for 94.6 million LPs. Integrated into the muODE simulator, it accelerated single trajectories 84-fold and 16-member ensembles 635-fold, and made adaptive Runge-Kutta integration affordable, reducing biomass errors 83-fold. Integrating 49 equally optimal flux policies in one batched run showed that alternative optima change predicted acetate 4.2-fold and shift community composition. manylp is open source: https://github.com/cumbof/manylp.

item.title: Learning to Design Convex Relaxations for Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by replacing hard nonconvex problems with convex surrogates that give valid bounds. Yet their design is still largely manual: a human expert must decide where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth is worth paying. We show that this design process can be learned. The method proposed in this paper, AutoConvexRelax, represents the symbolic formulation of a nonconvex problem as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions. It then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem-specific relaxation trajectories as the formulation evolves. We prove that finite action sequences generated by the learned policy preserve relaxation validity under explicit domain, occurrence-context, and representation-consistency conditions. We further establish computable error bounds for mixed relaxations and sufficient conditions for feasible recovery and global-optimality certification. As a first instantiation, we apply the method to nonconvex quadratic problems and fractional problems. On 241 benchmark quadratic instances, the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%. Its mean lower bound is 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations on the normalized comparison metric, while it uses substantially smaller formulations. The learned policy retains this trade-off on fractional instances and reaches near-semidefinite bounds on beamforming and sensor-network localization instances. These results suggest that convex relaxation design can move from a fixed handcrafted choice to an automated learning process that adapts to problem structures. Code is available at https://github.com/auto4opt/AutoConvexRelax.

item.title: Beyond Aggregate Drift: Optimal Client-Specific Windows in Federated Learning
item.description: We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one. We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[ R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,σ_m\sqrt{γ_m/λ_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $σ_m$, arrival rate $λ_m$, and drift rate $γ_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients. A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.

item.title: KKT Residual Sliding Manifolds: A Projection-Free Structured Finite-Time Solver for Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation
item.description: Nonlinear Constrained Optimisation (NCO) requires simultaneous satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Existing methods enforce these conditions through projections, penalties, barriers, or sequential approximations, potentially introducing computational complexity and convergence difficulties. For nonconvex problems, a KKT point need not be a local optimum. This paper reformulates NCO as stabilisation of a unified KKT sliding residual manifold and develops SM-KKT, a projection-free solver. Stationarity, equality feasibility, and regularised Fischer-Burmeister complementarity are integrated into a unified residual system, with complementarity encoding inequality feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness. The manifold's zero set is shown to be equivalent to the KKT conditions. The required Jacobian saddle-point inertia is characterised and shown, under stated assumptions, to be equivalent to the simultaneous satisfaction of the Linear Independence Constraint Qualification (LICQ) and Second-Order Sufficient Condition (SOSC). This characterisation establishes local stability of the structured correction algorithm under these conditions and distinguishes nondegenerate locally optimal KKT solutions from points failing second-order optimality. SM-KKT computes structured primal--dual corrections and applies a discrete sliding reaching law to drive the KKT residual into a prescribed boundary layer in finite time. Four nonlinear benchmarks show recovery of reference constrained optima with KKT residuals below $10^{-6}$, earlier boundary-layer reaching, and favourable KKT accuracy compared with projected primal-dual, augmented-Lagrangian, quadratic-penalty, and log-barrier baselines.

item.title: Homogenization of an optimal control problem for a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a 3D perforated domain
item.description: We study the homogenization of an optimal control problem governed by a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a periodically perforated three-dimensional domain. The obstacles are Lipschitz sets of size $\varepsilon^α$, $α>3$, where $\varepsilon$ is the period. The fluid satisfies the no-slip condition on the outer boundary and the free-slip condition on the obstacles, the phase-field equation contains a source term, and the convective term carries a pore-scale Reynolds number that tends to zero as $\varepsilon\to0$. The control is a distributed body force, and the cost functional tracks the velocity in $L^2$ and the order parameter in $H^1$. Since uniqueness of weak solutions of the state system is not known for fixed $\varepsilon$, the control-to-state relation is multivalued, and we pose the microscopic problems over control-state pairs. We prove the existence of microscopic optimal pairs and the sequential $Γ$-convergence of the cost functionals to the cost functional of a control problem governed by the unsteady Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system on the full domain. As a consequence, the optimal values converge, every cluster point of microscopic optimal pairs is optimal for the homogenized problem, and the optimal controls converge strongly along the corresponding subsequences. The $\liminf$ inequality follows from the homogenization of the state system, including the strong convergence of the gradients of the order parameter. Only the recovery sequence requires uniqueness of weak solutions of the homogenized system, which we prove when the outer boundary is of class $C^{2,1}$.

item.title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget
item.description: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

item.title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
item.description: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

item.title: The $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance via $3\times3$ block matrices (with application to $p$-Bures-Wasserstein barycenters)
item.description: We study the $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance $D_p(A,B)=(\mathrm{tr}\,A^p+\mathrm{tr}\,B^p-2\|A^{1/2}B^{1/2}\|_p^p)^{1/2}$ on positive semidefinite matrices; it equals the Bures-Wasserstein distance for $p=1$, and the Hilbert-Schmidt distance for $p=2$. We prove that $D_p$ is a metric for every $1\le p\le2$, by proving a stronger 2014 conjecture of Lin and van den Driessche on $3\times3$ block matrices. Our main tool is a partition inequality for Schatten norms, proved by complex interpolation. We also characterize Fréchet means for $D_p$ by a fixed-point equation and prove geometric convergence of the associated iteration.

item.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
item.description: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrubeš that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $Θ(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.

item.title: An Efficient, Lean 4 Verified Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Membership in Pedigree Polytopes
item.description: The set \(P_{n}\) consists of the characteristic vectors of pedigrees, which are combinatorial encodings in one-to-one correspondence with Hamiltonian cycles. For \(n \geq 4\) and \(τ_{n} = \binom{n}{3}-1\), the Membership Problem for the Pedigree Polytope (M3P) asks whether a given vector \(X \in \mathbb{Q}^{τ_{n}}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{conv}(P_n)\). This paper gives a complete account, with the full proof statements and machine-verified Lean~4 certificates, of the necessary and sufficient (\NS) condition established in Chapter~5 of \emph{Pedigree Polytopes: New Insights on Computational Complexity of Combinatorial Optimisation Problems} (Arthanari, 2023): membership of $X$ in $\mathrm{conv}(P_n)$ is characterised by the feasibility, at every stage $k=4,\dots,n-1$, of a recursively constructed layered network, together with, when needed, a multicommodity flow problem $\mathrm{MCF}(k-1)$ achieving its maximum possible flow $z_{\max}$. We present the construction, the \NS{} condition itself, and the proofs of this characterisation, together with the resulting polynomial-time algorithm for M3P. Both directions of the \NS{} condition --- sufficiency and necessity (the multicommodity-flow feasibility argument of the book's Chapter~5) --- are machine-verified in Lean~4/Mathlib4 with zero unresolved \texttt{sorry}s in either dependency chain. The \NS{} characterisation therefore follows directly from the two machine-checked implications. The complete Lean~4 project is publicly available. A companion introductory article (arXiv:2507.09069) presents the same material for a broader readership, without the Lean~4 verification; the present paper adds full statements, proof sketches, and the complete machine-checked certificates.

item.title: Nonlinear Feedback Control in High Dimensions using the Polynomial-Polynomial Regulator
item.description: We consider the problem of computing Taylor approximations to the optimal feedback law and value function for infinite-horizon finite-dimensional nonlinear optimal control problem---also known as Al'brekht's method. The scalability of existing Al'brekht-based approaches to computing approximate solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the optimal control problem has been severely limited by computational resources. The computational time issue has been partially mitigated by recent works leveraging tensor-structure to develop efficient numerical methods. However, RAM requirements still have remained a major hindrance to scaling beyond state dimensions of a few hundred or low thousands. We propose an acceleration to compute the expensive higher-order terms in a reduced space, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. A fast and scalable \textsc{Matlab} implementation is provided open-source for general purpose use, with the ability to accommodate arbitrary polynomial nonlinearities in the control-affine state equation, as well as polynomial state-dependence in the cost function, and the ability to handle systems in generalized form with a non-identity mass matrix, such as finite element models. Combined with the exploitation of sparsity and modern low-rank Riccati solvers, this permits computing approximations to polynomial feedback laws based on Al'brekht's method in hundreds of thousands of states.

item.title: A Mean Field Model of Consumption Inertia and Keeping Up with the Joneses
item.description: Households compare their living standard with others' and dislike changing it. We study consumption and investment when felicity depends on consumption relative to a benchmark, the population's geometric average consumption, and cuts in felicity weigh more than increases. Asset returns are exogenous. For finitely many types and arbitrary initial wealth and inherited standards, a mean field equilibrium exists under a weak interaction condition, and for fixed budget multipliers the benchmark is the fixed point of a contraction. In a complete market with common risk, a mean field equilibrium at empirical type frequencies is an exact Nash equilibrium of the finite game, for any preferences over relative consumption. We bound the gain from deviating when plans computed at another composition are used. We compute equilibria in which groups with different wealth, inherited standards, and loss aversion revise spending at different dates. With identical households and common risk, the unique symmetric equilibrium is the policy of a single loss averse household with modified curvature. In a baseline example, ignoring the inherited standard costs up to 17% of wealth, while small errors about the composition of the reference group cost less than 0.5%.

item.title: Online Submodular Welfare Maximization: Computation is not the Bottleneck
item.description: We revisit the online submodular welfare maximization problem (OSW), a vast generalization of numerous well-studied online allocation problems, including online bipartite matching, display ads and AdWords. A natural greedy OSW algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $1/2$ [LLN06], and $1-1/e$ under i.i.d. arrivals [KPV13]. Both bounds are tight for polynomial-time algorithms unless NP=RP [KPV13]. The information-theoretic limits for OSW, in contrast, remained open. This prompted researchers to ask for tighter upper bounds [Mehta13] or conjecture the existence of better-competitive (slow) algorithms [Huang23, LTX+23, CHS24, Huang2024, HTW24}. We resolve Mehta's question and refute the subsequent conjectures, proving that the greedy algorithm is in fact tight for both adversarial and i.i.d. arrivals, regardless of computation time. Seemingly contradicting recent $(1-1/e)$-competitive fractional algorithms for OSW [HJP+24,Patton26], we show that this impossibility even holds for fractional algorithms, provided their outputs correspond to marginals that are roundable in hindsight. Conceptually, our proofs can be seen as identifying that a bottleneck for OSW, even under (deterministic) adversarial arrivals, is the inherently random notion of correlation gap [ADSY12].

item.title: Admissibility-Preserving Constraint Lifting for Conditional Deadbeat Control of Discrete-Time Nonlinear Systems
item.description: This paper presents a constraint-enforcing control framework for a class of discrete-time strict- feedback nonlinear systems. The objective is to guarantee closed-loop stability while ensuring forward invariance of a prescribed safe set defined by state constraints. The pro- posed approach transforms the constrained control problem into an equivalent unconstrained one through smooth constraint-lifting mappings constructed using strictly increasing sigmoid functions. Controller synthesis is then performed in the lifted coordinates, enabling recursive backstepping design while preserving the admissibility of the constrained states. Conditions on the controller gains are derived to guarantee both asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system and forward invariance of the admissible domain of the lifting functions. The analysis also establishes a conditional deadbeat property for the second backstepping step once the system trajectory enters a region in which the lifting-domain admissibility conditions are satisfied. Numerical simulations of a constrained Roup oscillator demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in enforcing state constraints while tracking a reference command.

item.title: Constraint-Lifted Sector-Constrained Guidance for Rear-Approach Interception
item.description: This paper develops a sector-constrained guidance (SCG) law for interception of a maneuvering target while maintaining a prescribed approach geometry. The line of sight is required to remain within a specified angular sector behind the target throughout the engagement, resulting in a state-constrained guidance problem. To enforce this constraint, the directional angle between the target heading and the line of sight is mapped from the prescribed sector to an unconstrained coordinate using a sigmoid diffeomorphism. A guidance law is then designed in the lifted coordinate to generate a desired transverse velocity and corresponding pursuer lead angle. The desired lead angle is tracked through an inner-loop turn-rate controller, which is implemented through the normal-acceleration command of a nonlinear point-mass model. This construction embeds the sector constraint directly into the guidance law and does not require online constrained optimization. Numerical simulations against a maneuvering target show that SCG achieves interception while maintaining the prescribed rear-sector constraint, including when the pursuer normal-acceleration command is subject to actuator saturation. Comparisons with proportional guidance under the same engagement conditions demonstrate that proportional guidance may achieve interception but does not maintain the prescribed directional constraint.

item.title: On the convexification of a bilinearly constrained set with a common variable
item.description: We study the convexification of sets defined by box constraints and bilinear inequality constraints in which all bilinear terms share a common variable. For this structured class of nonconvex sets, we provide a complete characterization of the extreme points of the convex hull and derive an explicit description of all facet-defining inequalities, thereby obtaining a full polyhedral description of the convex hull. In addition, we develop a polynomial-time separation algorithm for the facet-defining inequalities and illustrate its effectiveness through examples. These results offer both structural insight into the geometry of the convex hull and algorithmic tools for identifying violated inequalities.

item.title: Regularity of the Price of Anarchy in Routing Games over the Multivariate Demand Space
item.description: We study the price of anarchy (PoA) in nonatomic routing games as a function of the full vector of origin--destination demands. We show that the Beckmann value function is continuously differentiable on the positive demand cone, with gradient equal to the equilibrium origin--destination cost vector; hence the PoA is continuously differentiable on the regular demand region. We prove that the nondifferentiability set has Lebesgue measure zero and, when every edge cost is strictly increasing or constant, is covered by countably many codimension-one submanifolds. Under the same cost structure, all equilibrium objects are cellwise as smooth as the edge costs. For affine costs, the exceptional sets become finite unions of lower-dimensional polyhedral cells linked by an exact scaling law, and the maximum of the PoA over a cell closure is attained on the cell boundary, generalizing the one-dimensional endpoint result. The theory is illustrated on the Sioux Falls benchmark network.

item.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
item.description: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

item.title: Optimal Synthesis on the Special Linear Group
item.description: We study the exponential map on the group of real two-by-two matrices with determinant one, endowed with a left-invariant Riemannian metric. Using the Euler-Poincaré equation and its linearization, we determine the conjugate and Maxwell times and identify a domain on which the exponential map is a global diffeomorphism onto the complement of the Maxwell stratum. This provides an alternative proof that the first Maxwell time coincides with the cut time. We obtain an explicit matrix description of the cut locus and characterize the globally minimizing geodesics. Furthermore, we analyze the first Maxwell-time function, determine its unique global minimum, and show that the injectivity radius is $\frac{π\sqrt{14}}{4}$. Finally, we characterize the intersection of the cut and conjugate loci and prove that every geodesic is equi-optimal.

item.title: Well-Posedness and Strong Convergence of Infinite-Dimensional Port-Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Gradient Dynamics
item.description: We establish a functional-analytic framework that justifies the LaSalle convergence argument outlined in [van der Schaft, 2026] on port-Hamiltonian primal-dual gradient dynamics for finite-horizon optimal control of linear systems. In addition to strict convexity of the running cost as in \cite{vanderSchaft2026PDGJuly}, our analysis requires global Lipschitz continuity of the cost gradient. This ensures that the nonlinear gradient operator is well-defined and Lipschitz on the entire underlying space. We establish global well-posedness of the optimizer dynamics: every initial value determines a unique global mild solution, and the associated solution operators form a contraction semigroup. Similar to [Gernandtand Schaller, 2025], this is proved using tools from maximal monotone operator theory. Assuming existence of an optimal solution, we combine a dissipation inequality with an infinite-dimensional LaSalle invariance principle to prove strong convergence of every trajectory with a relatively compact positive orbit to the unique optimal state, control, and costate. Moreover, we present a sufficient condition for compactness through uniform control regularity and show that convergence holds for all initial states. Finally, we present an example with a strictly but not strongly convex running cost for which every mild solution converges strongly to the unique equilibrium, while no global exponential estimate uniformly over initial values can be obtained.

item.title: On the Complexity of Finding Stationary Points of p-th Order Hölder Smooth Functions in One Dimension
item.description: We study the query complexity of finding an an $\varepsilon$-stationary points of a one-dimensional non-convex function whose $p$-th derivative is $β_p$-Hölder continuous. We determine the optimal complexity for deterministic and randomized algorithms and for oracles that return only derivatives, only function values, or full local information. Randomness provably helps when only derivatives are available, function values help in all cases, and higher-order derivatives never do. Together with known results in higher dimensions, this shows how these benefits depend on the dimension. Our deterministic lower bound also implies that the optimal accuracy exponents of objective-function-free adaptive regularization of order $p$ (OFFAR$p$) in every dimension $d\ge1$ and of deterministic gradient-only trapping in dimension $d=2$.

item.title: Some remarks on nonexistence in the Gamow liquid drop model
item.description: In this paper we deal with the celebrated Gamow liquid drop model, namely, for $m>0$, $N\geq 2$ and $α\in (0,N)$, we study the problem \[ \min\Big\{P(Ω)+ V_α(Ω) : Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^N,\;|Ω|=m\Big\}\,, \] and focus mostly on the nonexistence of minimizers for large masses. First we show that any possible minimizer in the asymptotic regime must satisfy an optimal thickness property. Eventually, in the simplified setting of sets made up as a tiling of cubes, we show that nonexistence occurs for large masses for the whole range of parameters $N\geq 2$ and $α\in (0,N)$.

item.title: Multiplicative Gradient Method for Log-Homogeneous Optimization: A Unified Mirror-Descent Framework
item.description: Consider the problems of computing $\ell_p$-Lewis weights, Kelly portfolios, D-optimal designs, general equilibria in Fisher markets, and optimal error exponents for channel coding in information theory. All of them can be formulated as optimization problems over the probability simplex, but except for the last one, the associated objective functions are neither Lipschitz continuous nor smooth, rendering existing first-order optimization algorithms and their guarantees not directly applicable. Nevertheless, first-order algorithms for solving these problems do exist in the literature and, perhaps surprisingly, look very similar, even though their interpretations, derivations, and analyses mostly appear unrelated. In this paper, we develop a framework unifying these results that captures their common problem structure through log-homogeneity and a novel second-order condition on the objective function, and identifies their common algorithmic pattern as multiplicative gradient methods. The framework recovers known algorithms and their optimization error guarantees for computing Kelly portfolios, D-optimal designs, optimal error exponents for channel coding in classical communication, $\ell_p$-Lewis weights with $p < 2$, and general equilibria in Fisher markets. To illustrate the insights provided by the framework, we further show that multiplicative gradient methods yield state-of-the-art performance guarantees for computing $\ell_p$-Lewis weights with $p > 2$ and optimal error exponents in classical-quantum communication. Both results are novel to the best of our knowledge.

item.title: Equilibria and consensus in discrete-time opinion dynamics with mixed weighted-averaging and weighted-median mechanisms
item.description: Opinion dynamics models relate interpersonal influence to consensus or persistent disagreement. We study a discrete-time model combining weighted-average and weighted-median updates on a fixed directed network. Individuals update synchronously with possibly different adjustment coefficients. We characterize equilibria through local balance conditions and opinion level sets, and establish convergence to a Lyapunov-stable equilibrium using nonexpansiveness and Krasnosel'skii--Mann theory. We define type-dependent cohesive sets: each weighted-average member assigns all its weight to the set, whereas each weighted-median member assigns at least one half. Consensus is reached from every initial condition if and only if no two such sets are disjoint. Otherwise, an open set of initial conditions leads to persistent disagreement. Replacing weighted-median individuals by weighted-average individuals preserves consensus whenever it is already guaranteed for all initial conditions. Four numerical studies examine the number and locations of weighted-average individuals. The frequency of reaching a prescribed consensus tolerance is nondecreasing with their fraction in the sampled ensembles, but individual realizations need not follow this trend.

item.title: Taming Nonconvexity with Epigraph Lifting
item.description: We consider inverse problems regularized by a trained neural network with \emph{convex activations} and \emph{unrestricted weights}. The resulting optimization problem is generally nonconvex, and gradient-based methods may converge to poor local minima. We introduce a \emph{penalized epigraph lifting} of the network and show that the lifted problem admits a \emph{difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition}. For Lipschitz continuous activations, we establish \emph{finite exactness}: the original objective is recovered exactly at a finite and explicitly computable penalty threshold $\barρ$. Building on this structure, we propose \emph{H-DC} (Homotopic DC), a homotopic scheme that solves a sequence of DC subproblems with increasing $ρ$, warm-starting each level from the previous solution. Numerical experiments on synthetic problems, a manifold denoiser regularizer, and image inpainting with a learned Mumford--Shah regularizer show that H-DC consistently escapes poor local minima and reaches solutions with lower objective values than gradient-based methods from the same initialization.

item.title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
item.description: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $Θ(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.

item.title: Towards learning-enhanced solvers for multi-parametric optimization
item.description: Neural networks (NNs) have been employed in various ways to accelerate the solution of multi-parametric optimization problems (OPs), which prominently arise in model predictive control (MPC). Early approaches focused on approximating the parametric solution (e.g., the optimal control law) directly by NNs. More recently, learning-based techniques have been used to emulate or enhance solver iterations. For the direct approximation of the parametric solution, it has been demonstrated that exploiting structural properties of the underlying OP facilitates the design of suitable NN architectures. In this paper, we show that structural analysis can also be leveraged to systematically integrate learning into classical optimization algorithms, thereby enhancing their performance. We formalize our concept for the case of multi-parametric quadratic programs (mpQPs), which frequently arise in linear-quadratic MPC, as a representative application. More precisely, we demonstrate that tailored NNs enable a parameter-dependent fine-tuning of the step sizes in a standard dual projected gradient scheme. The design of the NNs is guided by the observation that optimal step sizes, which permit obtaining the exact optimal solution in finitely many iterations, are piecewise constant functions over the parameter space (e.g., the state space in MPC). We establish key theoretical properties of the proposed approach and illustrate its effectiveness in a numerical case study.

item.title: Scalable Identification of Physics-Based and Neural Dynamics from Partial Measurements
item.description: We present a scalable method for identifying nonlinear dynamics from partial measurements, supporting physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. We use the Prediction Error Method (PEM) coupled with state estimation performed by a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme, which can account directly for general nonlinear dynamics. This results in a bi-level optimization problem that scales poorly with increasing model parameters. To improve computational efficiency, we derive a reformulation that avoids explicit parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploits the temporal structure of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical comparisons show up to a $215\times$ speedup in hypergradient evaluation. Racing-vehicle simulations demonstrate accurate prediction and physical-parameter recovery in tire-force identification. Real-world data show that the gray-box model improves prediction accuracy with a neural residual while retaining physical interpretability.

item.title: Minimal time for heat observability on almost-Riemannian surfaces
item.description: We determine the minimal observation time for the heat equation on a closed almost-Riemannian surface, for a class of observation sets leaving sufficiently thin collars around simple Baouendi-Grushin circles. The structure and density are analytic near these circles, and the coefficients may depend on both variables. The formula is expressed through a complex phase describing concentration near the singular set and extends the thresholds known for separated models. Regular unobserved regions away from the circles do not change this time, provided all other singularities are observed. For singular circles of constant bracket step greater than two, local analyticity implies failure of observability at every time for observation sets at positive distance. We also construct quasimodes concentrated near simple singular circles, with exponentially small errors. Their superpositions give a lower bound for the Schrödinger observation time.

item.title: Preconditioned Latent Variable Proximal Point Method for Optimal Control Problems with Control Constraints
item.description: The latent variable proximal point (LVPP) method solves optimization problems in function spaces with pointwise constraints by a sequence of smooth subproblems whose iterates are strictly feasible. We apply it to linear-quadratic elliptic optimal control problems. Control and observation are distributed but may be restricted to subdomains. We prove that the LVPP subproblems are well posed in appropriate function spaces, that the iteration converges for every sequence of proximity parameters with divergent sum, and that it delivers the Lagrange multiplier of the constraint as a by-product. We interpret the Newton step for the LVPP subproblem as a linear-quadratic optimal control problem with a spatially varying control cost, and we show that Newton's method converges locally quadratically. The Newton systems are solved by the minimal residual method with a block-diagonal preconditioner. We prove that the spectrum of the Newton operator with respect to the inner product defined by the preconditioner is bounded independently of the proximity parameter, the iterate, the mesh and the observation and control domains. The results are combined into a complete algorithm, and tested in numerical experiments.

item.title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
item.description: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

item.title: Globally Convergent Block Coordinate Descent Algorithms for Semi-Nonnegative Independent Component Analysis
item.description: We propose a subgradient-based block coordinate descent (BCD-SubG) framework for nonconvex optimization over products of probability simplices and a closed feasible set, motivated by semi-nonnegative independent component analysis (Semi-NNICA). Elementary column transformations are used to preserve simplex feasibility, while first-order information guides block and pair selection. We establish the global convergence of BCD-SubG using a constrained Lojasiewicz inequality; additional eventual-interiority conditions yield stationary limits and convergence rates. We then specialize BCD-SubG to the direct-fit and indirect-fit Semi-NNICA models and derive explicit updates that ensure global convergence without further assumptions. For both models, eventual interiority also yields stationary limits and convergence-rate estimates. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and simulated magnetic resonance spectroscopy data show generally lower recovery errors and shorter wall-clock times than the tested Semi-NNICA baselines. Joint diagonalization experiments further demonstrate lower final objective values.

item.title: On the Stability of Power Systems with AI Data Centers: A Multi-Equilibrium Switched DAE Framework
item.description: The rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) data centers is introducing dynamic loads into power transmission systems as GPU clusters switch between computational phases with distinct power demands. These dynamics are naturally modeled by switched affine differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), where each mode induces a different equilibrium and consistency space. We study their stability using control and hybrid systems tools. Differential projectors derived from the quasi-Weierstrass form yield an equivalent hybrid representation, from which we characterize the $ω$-limit set and establish Lyapunov conditions for practical stability with an explicit $\mathcal{KL}$ bound accounting for switching-induced resets. For stochastic inference workloads, we use Foster--Lyapunov techniques to establish probabilistic uniform global recurrence under mode-dependent dwell times and transition probabilities. The framework is validated on the IEEE 39-bus transmission network with co-located AI data centers using high-fidelity electromagnetic transient simulations of deterministic training and stochastic inference workloads.

item.title: Matching Full-Hessian Oracle Complexity for Nonconvex--Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization
item.description: We characterize the oracle complexity of finding first-order stationary points in smooth nonconvex--strongly-concave (NC--SC) minimax optimization when each query provides the full Hessian in addition to the function value and gradient. For $Φ(x)=\max_y f(x,y)$, assume that $f$ has an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, a $ρ$-Lipschitz Hessian, and is $μ$-strongly concave in $y$. Let $κ=L/μ$, let $Δ$ denote the initial value gap, and define $r=ρκ^{3/2}\varepsilon/L^2$. We establish matching deterministic upper bounds and randomized lower bounds, up to logarithmic factors and additive initialization costs. When the leading term dominates initialization, the resulting minimax complexity is \[ \widetildeΘ\!\left( \frac{ΔL}{\varepsilon^2}Ψ_κ(r) \right), \qquad Ψ_κ(r)= \begin{cases} r^{1/2}, & 0<r\le 1,\\ r^{2/7}, & 1<r<κ^{7/4},\\ \sqrtκ, & r\geκ^{7/4}. \end{cases} \] Despite the stronger oracle, the optimal complexity exhibits a nontrivial dependence on accuracy, conditioning, and Hessian smoothness. In particular, these regimes exhibit accuracy dependencies $\varepsilon^{-3/2}$, $\varepsilon^{-12/7}$, and $\varepsilon^{-2}$, respectively. The upper bounds combine second-order regularity estimates for a saddle Moreau envelope with certified accelerated reduced-dual solves and amortized warm starts. The lower bounds combine an all-derivative lift with a serial composition of private-handle constructions, using hard instances chosen independently of the algorithm's realized random seed. The resulting characterization quantifies improvements over the classical first-order benchmark under gradient smoothness alone and identifies the regime in which that benchmark is recovered.

item.title: A Deterministic $0.401$-Approximation for Non-monotone Submodular Maximization under Matroid Constraints
item.description: Submodular maximization arises in a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems and has been extensively studied from the perspective of approximation algorithms. For maximizing nonnegative, non-monotone submodular functions subject to a matroid constraint, randomized algorithms achieve a $0.401$-approximation, whereas obtaining comparable deterministic guarantees remains challenging. In this paper, we present a deterministic $0.401$-approximation algorithm in the exact value and independence oracle model, improving upon the previous deterministic guarantee of $(0.385-\varepsilon)$ \cite{ChenGLSZ2026}. Our algorithm builds on the extended multilinear extension and provides a deterministic implementation of the recursive guided framework underlying the randomized $0.401$-approximation algorithm. The main technical ingredient is a direction oracle supported on at most two partitioned matroid bases. This oracle simultaneously satisfies the growth condition required by the extended-multilinear update and an approximate stationarity condition needed to construct the recursive guides. The resulting finite-support representation enables exact evaluation of the relevant expectations and marginal values without random sampling. The algorithm uses polynomially many value- and independence-oracle queries.

item.title: Venusian Radio Occultation Constellation Design and Reconfiguration Problems: A Benders Decomposition Approach
item.description: Driven by the scientific value of Venusian atmospheric studies, numerous missions, such as Magellan and Venus Express, have relied on single-spacecraft radio occultation (RO) experiments. Despite their proven success, data throughput is inherently limited by the use of a single transmitter and its relative geometry with respect to Earth-based receivers. Therefore, the literature proposes leveraging a constellation of spacecraft to increase RO measurement opportunities and improve spatial and temporal coverage; however, current efforts impose strict simplifying assumptions that limit their applicability and responsiveness to complex mission narratives. Beyond initial constellation design, evolving mission objectives may require event-based constellation reconfiguration during operations. To address both design and operational needs, we propose two problems formulated as integer linear programs: the RO Constellation Configuration Design Problem and the RO Constellation Reconfiguration Problem. Further, we address the programs' solution-space explosion with a Benders decomposition approach. Numerical experiments show the applicability of our problems for constellation configuration design, tackle the full mission pipeline, transitioning from global atmospheric profiling to on-demand regional profiling above areas of volcanic interest, and show that the Benders decomposition approach efficiently obtains high-quality solutions to large-scale instances.

item.title: Calibrated $α$-Barycenters for Multiobjective $f$-Divergence Optimization
item.description: Matching one distribution to many targets can require repeated evaluations of every target. CAL-$α$-MODM aggregates a nonlinear predictor into one barycenter, calibrates its residual derivatives, and checks steps against the original $f$-divergence objective. Under smoothness assumptions, calibration controls parameter-step model error without requiring targets to be close to the model. Exact-oracle stationarity and local convergence guarantees are established. At common matching, canonical geometry cancels the leading quadratic iteration error, giving cubic convergence with second-order calibration and sufficiently accurate inner solves. High-precision experiments support this prediction. Sensitivity-based initialization also accelerates preference continuation along regular stationary branches. On 300-target Jensen--Shannon problems, CAL-p2 achieves median paired speedups of $3.15\times$ over L-BFGS and $1.10\times$ over second-order Direct-TR, across 23/25 and 24/25 objective-comparable stationary pairs. The savings arise when cheaper predictor queries offset calibration overhead.

item.title: Matching Complexity for Second-Order Stationary Point with Sample Reuse
item.description: We consider stochastic nonconvex optimization with sample-wise Lipschitz gradients and Hessians, and reusable opaque sample handles. Gradient and complete-Hessian evaluations are charged separately, including both endpoints of a same-sample difference. For fixed positive problem parameters and in the high-dimensional worst case, we prove that the minimax total derivative-query complexity of finding an $(\varepsilon,γ)$-second-order stationary point is \begin{equation*} \widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-3}+γ^{-3}). \end{equation*} The upper bound combines curvature-first randomly signed negative-curvature steps with binary-ancestor derivative estimators; a truncated increment estimate charges predictable drift linearly and martingale motion quadratically. The curvature lower bound uses a deterministic smooth bounded-gradient chain, a radial barrier, and a random rotation. The new first-order lower bound is specifically robust to persistent sample reuse and to complete-Hessian access. It uses a slowly parameterized conservative sign chain, a third-order reverse stick-breaking localization inequality, and stateful relative-entropy accounting for reusable handles. Thus the total rate is near-optimally matched for every relation between $\varepsilon$ and $γ$.

item.title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
item.description: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.

item.title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
item.description:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $

x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.

item.title: A Composite Bayesian Risk--Distributionally Robust Optimization Model for Stochastic Programming with Elliptical Distribution Ambiguity
item.description: We study a stochastic optimization problem in which the random vector follows a semiparametric elliptical distribution with unknown location and shape parameters and an unspecified radial distribution. Assuming that the decision maker only has access to samples of the random vector, we develop a framework to jointly address parameter uncertainty and distributional ambiguity arising from this composite structure. To update the posterior distribution of the parameters, a key challenge is that the density of an elliptical distribution depends on the unknown radial distribution, and hence conventional likelihood-based Bayesian inference is infeasible. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel estimating-equation-based Gibbs inference framework that updates posterior distributions of model parameters solely through estimating equations. For elliptical distributions, we construct a pair of estimating equations for the location and shape parameters that are invariant to the radial component, which enables posterior learning without specifying the density. For the distributional uncertainty, we construct an ambiguity set for the radial distribution by transforming observed samples into pseudo-samples of the radial variable. Combining the above components, we formulate a composite Bayesian risk--distributionally robust optimization model, in which the inner problem captures worst-case radial distributions within the ambiguity set, and the outer problem evaluates the decision risk induced by the parameter uncertainty through a user-specified risk measure. We further develop a cutting-plane algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach provides substantial performance improvements over benchmark methods, including sample average approximation and distributionally robust optimization.

item.title: Extragradient and Past Extragradient Methods for $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz Variational Inequalities
item.description: Variational inequalities (VIs) capture a broad class of optimization problems central to modern machine learning, including min-max optimization and equilibrium computation in multiplayer games. Traditionally, algorithms for solving VIs, such as Extragradient (EG) and Past Extragradient (PEG), have been analyzed under the standard $L$-Lipschitz assumption. However, this condition is often overly restrictive, and recent works have instead turned to the more relaxed $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz setting. Existing guarantees for $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz VIs require a quasi-sharpness condition [Vankov et al., 2024], while monotone guarantees for EG cover only unconstrained root finding [Choudhury and Loizou, 2025]. In this work, we provide the first convergence guarantees for EG and PEG for monotone $(L_0,L_1)$-Lipschitz VIs. We also improve upon prior convergence guarantees for strongly monotone VIs by supporting larger stepsizes in the constrained setting and eliminating exponential dependence on the initial distance from the solution for convergence rates in the unconstrained setting. Lastly, we propose line-search variants for when Lipschitz parameters are unknown. Numerical experiments complement our theoretical results and demonstrate the practical efficacy of our methods.

item.title: Solution Set Dimensions in Convex Optimization and Primal-Polar Facial Signatures
item.description: We study the possible dimensions of solution sets in linearly perturbed convex optimization problems and their behavior under convex duality. The dimensions of solution sets and inverse solution sets capture two complementary forms of nonuniqueness: that of optimal solutions for a given perturbation, and that of perturbations for which a given point is optimal. Although these two families are linked by Fenchel conjugacy, we show that their collections of dimensions can be prescribed independently for finite supercoercive convex functions. As a geometric consequence, we prove that the facial dimension signatures of a convex body and its polar can be prescribed independently. The connection between these two realization results is obtained by homogenizing the epigraphs of a function and its conjugate. In contrast, under simultaneous facial exposedness, we establish a dimensional obstruction relating the smallest positive proper face dimensions of the body and its polar. These results resolve two open questions posed by Roshchina and Tunçel.

item.title: Decision-Making in Digital Twins: Optimization, Control, and Learning
item.description: A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical system, continuously updated with data from the physical system, enabling dynamic information exchange and decision-making. This bidirectional interaction, which distinguishes digital twins from conventional simulation models, introduces new challenges to simulation-based optimization, control, and learning. This paper reviews recent developments in decision-making methodologies motivated by digital twins. We focus on three interconnected areas: simulation optimization, sequential decision making, and risk-aware decision making. For simulation optimization, we discuss data-driven simulation optimization under input uncertainty, streaming input data, decision-dependent observations, and limited computational and data-collection resources. For sequential decision making, we review the connections among digital twins, stochastic optimal control, and reinforcement learning, with emphasis on Bayesian approaches that update models and policies as new information becomes available. For risk-aware decision making, we discuss distributionally robust and Bayesian risk formulations as alternative approaches for addressing model uncertainty. Throughout the paper, we emphasize the common problem of making decisions while the underlying model is being updated. We conclude by identifying research challenges and opportunities.

item.title: Matching Randomized Bounds for Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Concave Optimization
item.description: We characterize the randomized component-oracle complexity of finite-sum nonconvex-concave optimization with a bounded dual domain. For $Φ(x)=\max_{y\in Y}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x,y)$, the goal is to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the Moreau envelope $Φ_{1/(2L)}$ with probability at least $2/3$ and a fixed query budget. Let $A=LΔ/\varepsilon^2$, $B=LD_Y/\varepsilon$, and $\bar B=\max\{1,B\}$, where $Δ$ bounds the initial primal gap and $D_Y$ bounds the dual diameter. For $A$ above a universal constant, the worst-case complexity is \[ \widetildeΘ\!\left(n+A\min\left\{ \sqrt n\,\bar B+\bar B^4,\ n^{3/4}\bar B\right\}\right). \] The bounds agree within constants for $B\le n^{1/4}$ and within one logarithm for larger $B$. Upper bounds require only mean-squared averaged smoothness and concavity of the average in the dual variable; lower bounds already hold under individual smoothness. The lower constructions cover adaptive component selection, arbitrary query norms, private randomization, and outputs that were never queried. A cone construction gives the small-diameter bound, while a serial branch construction and balanced replication give the remaining two regimes. On the upper side, a persistent estimator with primal averaging complements accelerated proximal dual steps equipped with an explicit primal certificate. The characterization takes the worst case over admissible known dual domains and finite dimensions.

item.title: Edge-preserving Bayesian neural networks via hierarchical sparsity-promoting priors
item.description: Recovering piecewise-smooth functions with jump discontinuities from noisy, indirect, and incomplete data is a central task in computational inverse problems. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with heavy-tailed weight priors have emerged as effective edge-preserving priors for such problems. However, posterior inference for these models remains computationally challenging, and existing approaches settle for point estimates obtained by directly optimizing heavy-tailed log-densities. We propose GSBL-BNNs, which model the neural network parameters hierarchically using sparsity-promoting priors from generalized sparse Bayesian learning (GSBL). The hierarchical formulation recovers several popular marginal priors, including Laplace and Student's $t$ (including Cauchy). A key modeling ingredient, novel among edge-preserving BNNs and native to the hierarchical formulation, couples each neuron's bias to its weights through a shared hyperparameter, so that the induced jump discontinuities are free to occur anywhere in the domain while the conditionally Gaussian structure underlying efficient inference is preserved. Furthermore, we develop a block-coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm for maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. This BCD approach alternates between standard network training with iteratively reweighted $\ell^2$-regularization and exact, closed-form hyperparameter updates for gamma and inverse gamma hyperpriors. Building on the BCD algorithm, we perform approximate Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification (UQ) using deep ensembles. Computational experiments---including signal denoising, deblurring, and inverting a two-dimensional hyperbolic conservation law--- show that GSBL-BNNs deliver accurate, edge-preserving reconstructions with built-in UQ. Compared with Gaussian- and Cauchy-BNNs, they yield more accurate predictive means and avoid overconfident uncertainty estimates.

item.title: Matching Randomized First-Order Bounds for Higher-Order Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: Does randomization improve the worst-case first-order complexity of nonconvex optimization when the objective is very smooth? We prove that, for every fixed finite integer $p\ge3$, finding an $\eps$-stationary point requires $Ω_p(\eps^{-5/3})$ exact value-and-gradient queries, even for $C^\infty$ objectives with initial gap at most one and simultaneous global Lipschitz budgets of one for derivatives of orders $1,\ldots,p$. Together with the known deterministic upper bound, this determines the accuracy exponent up to a single logarithmic factor. The lower bound holds for unrestricted adaptive randomized algorithms, unbounded query locations, and outputs that need not have been queried. One algorithm-independent hard distribution suffices in dimension $O_p(\eps^{-47/3})$. The construction combines a block-chain potential with an exact quartic core, repeated quadratic spectra, and two static Gaussian tensor perturbations. A scheduled Haar argument controls the entire adaptive query span. An innovation-only Gaussian comparison then bounds exact transcript information without assuming finite precision or a minimum query separation. This establishes the $5/3$ randomized accuracy barrier under every prescribed finite smoothness order, extending the previously matched third-order case.

item.title: A Feasible Direction Method with Active-Set Identification for Derivative-Free Optimization
item.description: We propose a model-based trust region method for derivative-free optimization with simulation-based inequality constraints. We are motivated by settings of simulation optimization in which both function evaluations at infeasible points may be unreliable and constraint evaluations are expensive. Our method maintains feasible incumbents and computes steps from a subproblem suitable for a feasible-direction method in order to encourage generation of feasible trial points. To reduce the computational cost of modeling the constraints, we describe an active-set estimation scheme that permits modeling with only a subset of constraints in each subproblem, as opposed to maintaining models of all constraints. We show that every limit point of the incumbents generated by our method is a Fritz-John point, and is additionally a KKT point under the Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification. Under standard nondegeneracy conditions, the active-set estimate identifies, within finite time, all constraints active at the limit point of the incumbents. Experiments on CUTEst problems show that our method generates feasible trial points far more often than a comparable SQP-based approach and solves more problems within a given budget with fewer function evaluations.

item.title: A Composite Representation Theorem for Solution Mappings in Regularized Composite Optimization with Applications to Hausdorff Lipschitz Stability
item.description: We study the geometry and stability of solution mappings in regularized composite optimization, allowing multiple minimizers. We establish a composite representation that separates optimal linear images from their corresponding primal solutions through an image mapping and a generalized basis pursuit mapping. Under a fiber-attainment condition, the image mapping admits a reduced optimization formulation; neither representation requires convexity. For convex regularizers, suitable qualification conditions yield a Fenchel-conjugate representation of the reduced value function and a geometric characterization of the generalized basis pursuit mapping through affine fibers and a fixed lifting set. Using these representations, we establish sufficient conditions for local Hausdorff Lipschitz continuity of possibly set-valued solution mappings. We further show that the primal-space sufficient conditions imply the corresponding image-space conditions, with an additional injectivity requirement arising in the former. The results cover $\ell_1$-type and structured piecewise linear-quadratic regularizers under suitable assumptions. For classical $\ell_1$ regularization, our approach recovers an existing stability result without a finite sign-pattern decomposition. Numerical examples illustrate the recovery of complete solution sets, including a case with a nonpolyhedral graph of the generalized basis pursuit mapping.
